title: Site overview
text:
### ops.ch01.s1 Site overview

1. Harborwick 3PL Ltd. operates a single logistics site in Port Sellow, Alveria. The site is a third-party warehouse for packed consumer goods — food, drugstore products and household items — stored and distributed for about twenty regular clients. Accuracy of stock on the rack against stock in the system is the operating principle of the whole site.

2. The site consists of one single-storey warehouse hall of 6,000 m2 with 10 m clear internal height, plus a small attached office annex. All goods handling, storage and value-added activities take place inside the hall. The office annex holds management, dispatch and welfare facilities and is separated from warehouse traffic.

3. The fenced yard outside the hall covers about 3,500 m2. It contains the access roads, manoeuvring areas for goods vehicles, eight dock doors at 1.2 m dock height, and a marked waiting area for drivers. Drivers wait in the waiting area and do not enter the hall. The yard is entered only through the controlled gate and exit is by the same route.

4. Operating hours are two shifts, Monday to Friday: morning shift 06:00-14:00 and afternoon shift 14:00-22:00. In peak season a Saturday morning overtime shift is added. One shift supervisor is in charge of the floor on every shift. About 38-40 people work on site across management, supervision, operations, stock control, dispatch and maintenance.

5. The hall floor is divided into six fixed zones, A to F, which structure all goods flow and all pedestrian and truck movements. Receiving, bulk storage, picking, dispatch, cold storage and services/control each have a defined footprint. No storage, staging or handling takes place outside its assigned zone.

6. Traffic inside the building uses a fixed aisle system. Main transport aisles are 4.0 m wide and serve forklifts, reach trucks and pallet jacks moving between zones and docks. Rack storage aisles in the bulk storage area are 3.0 m wide. Aisles are kept clear at all times and are not used for staging or temporary storage.

7. Pedestrians move only on designated walkways. Pedestrian walkways are 1.2 m wide and are physically separated from truck traffic by yellow barriers. Marked crossings connect walkways across transport aisles and at the docks. Pedestrian zones, crossings and dock ramps are shared areas where vehicles and people meet and are marked accordingly.

8. Speed limits apply to all powered equipment and vehicles and are enforced. The limit is 8 km/h inside the building and 15 km/h in the yard. Wherever people and trucks meet — in marked pedestrian zones, at crossings and on the dock ramps — the limit is 5 km/h. Limits are signposted at the gate, at the hall entrances and at each shared area.

9. On entry, every person reports to the designated entry point, wears the required personal protective equipment for the warehouse floor, and follows the walkways and crossings. Visitors and drivers remain in their assigned areas. Any person entering the floor must understand the hall and yard layout, the zone boundaries, the one-way use of inbound and outbound docks, and the speed and walkway rules before starting work.

title: Zones A-F
text:
1. The 6,000 m2 hall is divided into six fixed zones, A to F, with marked floor boundaries and signage. Each zone has one defined purpose and its own footprint. All goods, equipment and activities stay in their assigned zone, and goods move between zones only in the sequence A to B/E/F to C to D.

2. Zone A — receiving, 800 m2, is located along inbound docks 1-4. It contains the unloading lanes, inspection tables, document-check stations and system booking points. All inbound vehicles are unloaded here and no inbound goods leave Zone A before documents are checked, quantities are counted, condition is inspected and the receipt is booked.

3. Zone B — bulk storage, 2,200 m2, is the main reserve storage area. It holds high-bay pallet racking with 2,400 pallet positions for full pallets replenishing picking and special storage. Each rack bay carries at most 2,700 kg. Outside racking, free block-stacking is permitted only up to 3 pallets high and 4.0 m total height, in marked stack positions clear of aisles and sprinklers.

4. Zone C — picking, 1,200 m2, holds the order-fulfilment faces. It contains ground-level pick faces and flow racks, fed by replenishment from Zone B. Only released replenishment stock and open customer orders are held here. Picking equipment, empty-pallet stacks for order build and scanner staging are located at the aisle ends so pick faces remain clear.

5. Zone D — dispatch, 900 m2, is the outbound staging area in front of outbound docks 5-8. It contains marked staging lanes per door, stretch-wrapping stations and final-check positions. Only wrapped, labelled and system-released pallets are staged here, allocated to their assigned outbound door and time slot. No unwrapped stock or inbound goods are held in Zone D.

6. Zone E — cold zone, 300 m2, is the enclosed chilled store for temperature-sensitive packed goods. It is held continuously between +2 °C and +8 °C, with continuous monitoring, audible alarms and a manual temperature verification each shift. Its doors are kept closed except for put-away, replenishment and checks, and only cold-chain goods and their handling equipment enter.

7. Zone F — services and control, 600 m2, holds value-added packing workstations, the quarantine area, and the returns-inspection area. It also contains the separate ventilated hazmat cage of 60 m2. Quarantine holds damaged and suspect goods after they are found the same day. Returns are inspected here before any decision on restock, rework or scrap. The hazmat cage is the only place hazmat may sit, at no more than 4,000 kg at a time.

8. Zone boundaries, walkways and transport aisles are permanently marked and separated by barriers where pedestrians and trucks meet. Inbound flow uses doors 1-4 through Zone A; outbound flow uses Zone D to doors 5-8. Drivers do not enter any zone and wait in the marked yard waiting area. Any change to zone layout, racking positions or staging lanes is recorded on the site plan before use.

title: Docks and yard
text:
1. The yard and docks are the only interface between road transport and the hall. The fenced yard of about 3,500 m2 contains the access road, trailer manoeuvring area, pedestrian routes to the office annex, eight dock doors at 1.2 m dock height, and a marked driver waiting area. Entry and exit are through the controlled gate on a fixed one-way circulation that keeps arriving and departing vehicles separate.

2. Dock doors have strictly separated directions. Doors 1-4 are inbound only and open directly into Zone A receiving. Doors 5-8 are outbound only and open directly from Zone D dispatch. No inbound unloading takes place at doors 5-8, and no outbound loading takes place at doors 1-4. The separation is marked on the floor, on the doors inside and outside, and on the site plan at the gate.

3. Every vehicle movement is assigned in advance by the dispatcher. The dispatcher books transport, allocates a door number and a time slot, and communicates it to the carrier before arrival. Trucks arriving without a slot, arriving early, or arriving at the wrong door wait in the marked waiting area until the dispatcher reassigns them. Shift supervisors and operators do not change door allocations on their own.

4. On arrival the driver reports to the gate, confirms door and slot, and proceeds to the waiting area or directly to the assigned door when called. Drivers remain in the cab during docking or, if required to leave the cab, remain in the marked waiting area and the marked dock-side pedestrian bay. Drivers never enter the hall, Zone A, Zone D, or any storage aisle.

5. Inbound docks 1-4 serve Zone A only. Trailers reverse to the assigned leveller, are chocked and secured, and unloading starts only after documents have been presented and checked. Unloaded goods stay in Zone A for counting, inspection and system booking. Nothing is moved to Zone B, E or F until booking is complete.

6. Outbound docks 5-8 serve Zone D only. Only wrapped, labelled and system-released pallets staged in the marked lane for that door are loaded. The dispatcher releases each load, confirms trailer identity and seal, and authorises departure. No pallet is added, removed or restaged after release without a new dispatcher instruction.

7. Each dock door has its own dock leveller, door seal, traffic light and chock point. Levellers bridge the 1.2 m dock height to the trailer bed and are operated only by trained operators. Doors remain closed when no trailer is docked. Dock ramps and the marked areas where pedestrians and trucks meet are 5 km/h zones; elsewhere the yard limit is 15 km/h.

8. Pedestrians in the yard use only the 1.2 m walkways physically separated by yellow barriers and the marked crossings to the office annex and waiting area. The manoeuvring area in front of the doors is a no-walk zone except on the marked crossings under supervisor escort. Forklifts do not enter the yard road except to cross at marked points, and pallet jacks do not leave the hall.

9. The yard is kept clear at all times. No storage, staging, pallet stacks, waste or empty equipment is placed in manoeuvring lanes, in front of doors, on crossings or in the waiting area. Snow, ice, spills and debris are cleared before docking resumes, and any damage to doors, levellers, barriers or markings is reported to the shift supervisor and the maintenance technician the same shift.

title: Management and supervision
text:
1. Harborwick 3PL Ltd. is run by the warehouse manager as the single accountable person for the whole site. The warehouse manager owns operations, safety and inventory accuracy, sets the way the six zones are used, and gives the final sign-offs where the rules require them. Where this manual requires manager approval, no other role may give it.

2. Day-to-day control of the floor is delegated to the shift supervisors. Two shift supervisors cover the two shifts, morning 06:00-14:00 and afternoon 14:00-22:00, Monday to Friday, plus the Saturday morning overtime shift in peak season when it is ordered. There is always one shift supervisor in charge of the floor on every working shift.

3. The shift supervisor on duty directs all floor staff during the shift: inbound operators in Zone A, forklift operators on transport and put-away, pickers in Zone C, dispatch work in Zone D, and work in Zones E and F as allocated. Stock controllers, dispatchers and the maintenance technician coordinate with the supervisor on timing and priorities, but the supervisor decides the order of floor work and the allocation of people and equipment.

4. The shift supervisor is the first point of response for any incident on the shift. In case of injury, damage, spill, temperature alarm, equipment fault or evacuation, the supervisor takes charge of the floor, stops work where needed, secures the area, calls the warehouse manager and external services as required, and ensures the incident report is completed and reviewed on that shift.

5. Handover between supervisors is direct and documented under PR-15. The outgoing supervisor briefs the incoming supervisor on work in progress, dock slots in progress, staffing, equipment status, quarantine and hazmat status, and any open incidents before the new shift starts work. The floor is never left without a named supervisor in charge.

6. The warehouse manager approves all overtime, authorises every new forklift operator before independent driving, and signs off the annual wall-to-wall stocktake results and any damaged-goods write-off above 500 EUR. The shift supervisor approves write-offs up to 500 EUR, the final disposition of inspected returns, and reviews every incident report from the shift.

7. The dispatcher owns dock scheduling for doors 1-4 inbound and doors 5-8 outbound and assigns every carrier a door and a time slot. Supervisors and operators do not change door allocations on their own and refer carriers without a valid slot to the dispatcher and the marked waiting area.

8. With about 38-40 people on site across management, supervision, operations, stock control, dispatch and maintenance, lines of authority stay short. Every person on the floor knows who the supervisor in charge is, follows that supervisor's instructions on sequencing and safety, and escalates doubts on stock, damage, safety or capacity to the supervisor and, through the supervisor, to the warehouse manager.

title: Operational roles
text:
1. Forklift operators, eight in total across both shifts, drive the powered handling fleet. They operate the 6 counterbalance forklifts and 4 reach trucks for transport, put-away, replenishment and loading, and the 8 electric pallet jacks for horizontal moves. They work only on equipment they are authorised for, only after the warehouse manager has authorised them as operators, and only after the documented daily check before first use.

2. Inbound operators, six in total, own the work in Zone A receiving at docks 1-4. They check delivery documents before unloading, unload assigned trailers, count quantities, inspect condition, and present goods for system booking under PR-01. They do not release goods to Zone B, E or F until booking is complete, and they keep inspection stations, unloading lanes and dock approaches clear.

3. Pickers, ten in total, work in Zone C against scanner tasks. They replenish-fed pick faces and flow racks, pick customer orders by scanner instruction, scan-verify every picked item before packing under PR-04, and move picked, labelled units to Zone D. They work from the 20 shared WMS scanners, keep pick faces clear, and report shortages, damage and location errors to the shift supervisor and stock controllers.

4. Stock controllers, two in total, own inventory accuracy day to day. They run the daily cycle counts on the rotating zone schedule, perform the mandatory second count before any adjustment, post adjustments only after recount under PR-08, and investigate differences between system and rack. They control quarantine bookings with returns staff, monitor Zone B, E and F accuracy, and prepare the annual wall-to-wall stocktake for manager sign-off.

5. Returns and packing staff, four in total, work in Zone F services and control. They receive returns within 14 days of delivery, inspect every unit, and propose restock, rework or scrap for supervisor approval under PR-07. They operate the value-added packing workstations, handle quarantine goods moved the same day they are found, and prepare damaged-goods cases for write-off decision.

6. The maintenance technician maintains all trucks, racking and dock equipment. He carries out planned checks and repairs on forklifts, reach trucks, pallet jacks, dock levellers, stretch wrappers and the cardboard baler, performs the monthly documented racking safety inspection, and logs every repair with date, equipment, fault and action. He stops and tags out unsafe equipment and reports it to the shift supervisor immediately.

7. Dispatchers, two in total, own transport and outbound release from the office annex. They book transport, assign every carrier a door and time slot for doors 1-4 inbound and 5-8 outbound, call trucks from the marked waiting area, and release outbound loads from Zone D under PR-06. They confirm trailer identity and seal on loading, authorise departure, and are the only roles that change dock allocations.

8. Floaters, two in total, cover absence and peak load across Zones A, C, D and F. They work as trained pickers, packers or inbound support as assigned by the shift supervisor in charge, follow the same zone, scanner and PPE rules as the role they fill, and do not drive forklifts or reach trucks unless separately authorised as forklift operators.

title: Approvals and sign-offs
text:
1. No operation moves past its control point without the fixed approval for that step. Documents are checked before unloading, booking is completed before put-away, replenishment is released before picking, loads are released before loading, and returns are inspected before any decision on restock, rework or scrap. Where this manual names an approver, no other role may substitute.

2. The warehouse manager gives the site-level sign-offs. The manager signs off the annual wall-to-wall stocktake results under PR-08, without which the stocktake is not closed. The manager signs off any damaged-goods write-off above 500 EUR under PR-09. No goods are scrapped, removed from stock or written off above that threshold without that signature.

3. Only the warehouse manager approves overtime. The Saturday morning overtime shift in peak season, any extension of the 06:00-14:00 or 14:00-22:00 shifts, and any additional hours for individuals require prior manager approval. Shift supervisors plan the floor within approved hours and escalate shortfalls instead of ordering overtime themselves.

4. Only the warehouse manager authorises new forklift operators. No person drives a counterbalance forklift, reach truck or electric pallet jack independently until the manager has authorised that person for that equipment type under PR-10. Authorisation is recorded before first use, and the documented check before first use each day is a condition of continued use, not a substitute for authorisation.

5. The shift supervisor in charge gives the shift-level approvals. The supervisor approves damaged-goods write-offs up to and including 500 EUR. Any case above that amount is secured, documented and passed to the warehouse manager the same day it is found. Split write-offs to stay below the threshold are not permitted.

6. The shift supervisor approves the final disposition of every inspected return under PR-07. Returns and packing staff inspect every unit returned within 14 days of delivery and propose restock, rework or scrap, but no returned unit is restocked, reworked, quarantined for scrap or released to Zone B, C or E until the supervisor has approved the proposal. Quarantine movements the same day they are found do not replace this approval.

7. The shift supervisor reviews every incident report from the shift under PR-14 and PR-15. Injury, near-miss, damage to racking or equipment, spill, cold-chain alarm, evacuation and any breach of speed, walkway or dock rules are reported to the supervisor in charge, documented before handover, and reviewed and countersigned by that supervisor before the next shift starts work.

8. The dispatcher owns dock scheduling and outbound release. The dispatcher assigns every carrier a door and time slot for doors 1-4 inbound and doors 5-8 outbound, calls trucks from the marked waiting area, releases each outbound load from Zone D under PR-06, and confirms trailer identity and seal before authorising departure. Supervisors and operators do not change doors, slots or released loads without a new dispatcher instruction.

9. Inventory adjustments follow the two-count rule with no exception. No adjustment is posted under PR-08 without a second count by a stock controller, and the annual stocktake result is valid only with manager sign-off. Racking remains in use only with the monthly documented safety inspection by the maintenance technician, and re-entry after any evacuation is permitted only after roll call at the assembly point by the north fence is complete.

title: Shift pattern
text:
1. Harborwick 3PL Ltd. operates on two fixed shifts, Monday to Friday. The morning shift runs 06:00-14:00 and the afternoon shift runs 14:00-22:00. These times govern all floor work in Zones A to F, all dock operations at doors 1-4 inbound and 5-8 outbound, and all movements of forklifts, reach trucks and pallet jacks. No regular work is scheduled outside these windows.

2. Each shift is a complete operating unit. The shift starts with briefing, equipment checks and confirmation of dock slots, and ends with clearing of aisles, securing of equipment and documented handover to the next shift under PR-15. Work in progress at 14:00 passes from the morning shift to the afternoon shift without stopping booked inbound and outbound slots, and work in progress at 22:00 is secured and recorded for the next morning.

3. There is always one named shift supervisor in charge of the floor on every working shift. The two shift supervisors cover the morning and afternoon shifts respectively, so the floor is never worked without a supervisor present. The supervisor directs floor staff, sequences zone work, coordinates with dispatchers and stock controllers, and takes charge of any incident response during that shift.

4. The total workforce of about 38-40 people is distributed across the two shifts to keep all zones covered. Forklift operators, inbound operators, pickers, returns and packing staff and floaters are rostered to mornings and afternoons so that Zone A receiving, Zone B put-away and replenishment, Zone C picking, Zone D dispatch and Zone F services can run in parallel. Stock controllers, dispatchers and the maintenance technician align their hours to support both shifts and the start-up and close-down tasks.

5. Shift changeover takes place at the fixed times of 06:00, 14:00 and 22:00. Operators do not leave the floor until the incoming supervisor has accepted handover and staffing for the next period is confirmed. Trucks docked across a changeover stay on their assigned door and slot under dispatcher control, and goods in Zone A awaiting booking, pallets in Zone D awaiting release, and replenishment tasks in Zone C remain under supervisor ownership until handed over.

6. In peak season a Saturday morning overtime shift is added. The Saturday shift is an overtime extension of the Monday to Friday pattern, used for backlog inbound, replenishment of pick faces and pre-staged outbound loads. Its hours, staffing and dock use are set in advance for that Saturday only and do not create a permanent third shift or weekend operation.

7. Only the warehouse manager approves overtime. The Saturday morning overtime shift, any extension of the 06:00-14:00 or 14:00-22:00 shifts, early starts, late finishes and any additional hours for individuals all require prior manager approval. Shift supervisors plan sequencing, multi-skilling and floater deployment within approved hours and escalate shortfalls to the manager instead of ordering overtime themselves.

8. Outside approved shift hours the hall is closed to handling. At the end of the afternoon shift, and at the end of any approved Saturday overtime shift, the supervisor in charge confirms that dock doors are closed, levellers are parked, powered equipment is keyed off and charged, quarantine and the hazmat cage are secured, temperature monitoring in Zone E continues, and the building is locked. No lone working, unsupervised driving or unsupervised loading takes place outside the approved pattern.

title: End-of-shift handover
text:
1. Every shift ends with a direct, documented handover from the outgoing shift supervisor to the incoming shift supervisor under PR-15. Handover is a face-to-face briefing on the floor with the handover record completed and signed by both supervisors. The floor is never left without a named supervisor in charge, and the incoming supervisor accepts ownership of all work, equipment and open incidents before the next period starts work.

2. Handover takes place at the fixed changeover times of 14:00 and 22:00, and at 06:00 at start-up, with additional handover at the end of any approved Saturday morning overtime shift. Operators do not leave their zones until the outgoing supervisor confirms release. Trucks docked across a changeover stay on their assigned door and slot, and goods in progress remain under supervisor ownership until the record is signed.

3. The handover record covers work in progress by zone. It states the status of unloading and inspection in Zone A at doors 1-4, put-away and replenishment tasks to and from Zone B, open scanner tasks and pick faces in Zone C, wrapped and staged pallets and released loads in Zone D at doors 5-8, temperature status and stock moves in Zone E, and packing, quarantine and returns inspection in Zone F including the hazmat cage quantity.

4. The handover record covers dock and transport status under dispatcher control. It lists carriers on doors, carriers waiting in the marked waiting area, completed and upcoming time slots for doors 1-4 inbound and doors 5-8 outbound, released outbound loads with trailer identity and seal where loading has started, and any delayed, early or unslotted arrivals referred to the dispatcher. Supervisors do not reassign doors or slots during handover.

5. The handover record covers people and equipment. It confirms staffing present, absences and floater deployment across Zones A, C, D and F, forklift, reach truck and pallet jack availability with faults and tag-outs, status of dock levellers, stretch wrappers, baler, WMS scanners and barriers, and the documented check before first use for trucks starting the new shift. Unsafe equipment stays tagged out and is named explicitly.

6. The handover record covers stock control and checks. It lists cycle counts completed and in progress on the rotating zone schedule, second counts outstanding, adjustments held pending recount, quarantine bookings, and the monthly racking inspection and quarterly evacuation drill where due. No adjustment is handed over as complete without its second count, and no stocktake result is handed over as closed without manager sign-off.

7. All incidents from the outgoing shift are handed over as open until reviewed and closed. Injury, near-miss, damage to racking, trucks or dock equipment, spill, cold-chain alarm, breach of speed, walkway, PPE or dock rules, and any evacuation or roll call at the assembly point by the north fence are entered in incident reports before handover. The outgoing supervisor briefs each event, action taken, area secured, and notifications made to the warehouse manager and dispatcher.

8. The shift supervisor in charge reviews every incident report from the shift before the next shift starts work. The outgoing supervisor countersigns completed reports and marks incomplete investigations as carried forward with owner and deadline. The incoming supervisor verifies that secured areas, quarantined goods moved the same day they were found, and stopped work remain secured until the investigation and supervisor review are complete.

9. At close-down at 22:00, and at the end of any Saturday overtime shift, handover additionally confirms securing of the site. The outgoing supervisor records that aisles are clear, dock doors 1-8 are closed with levellers parked, powered equipment is keyed off and on charge, quarantine and the 60 m2 hazmat cage are locked, Zone E monitoring between +2 °C and +8 °C continues with alarms active, and the hall and gate are locked. The record is filed in the shift file for audit and for the warehouse manager's review.

title: Per-shift checks
text:
### ops.ch03.s3 Per-shift checks

1. Every shift starts with serviceability checks before productive work begins and ends with a securing check before handover. The shift supervisor in charge owns the checks for that shift, assigns who carries them out in Zones A to F and at doors 1-8, and does not release trucks, docks or pick faces until the checks are confirmed. Results are recorded in the shift file and carried into the PR-15 handover.

2. Powered trucks are checked before first use each day with a documented check, and their status is re-verified at each shift start. The 6 counterbalance forklifts rated at 2.5 t, the 4 reach trucks rated at 1.6 t and the 8 electric pallet jacks are inspected for brakes, steering, lights, horn, seat belt, forks, chains, wheels, battery charge and leaks, plus the 12 hand pallet jacks for wheels, forks and hydraulics. Any fault is reported to the shift supervisor and the maintenance technician immediately, and the truck is tagged out until repaired and logged.

3. Only authorised operators drive after checks. The supervisor confirms at shift start that every driver on forklifts, reach trucks and electric pallet jacks has been authorised by the warehouse manager under PR-10. No licence, no truck. The 20 shared WMS scanners are counted, signed out, tested for login and scan function, and faulty units are swapped before picking in Zone C begins.

4. Docks, doors and yard are checked at shift start and continuously during the shift. Each of the 8 dock doors at 1.2 m dock height, its leveller, seal, traffic light and chock point is confirmed operational and damage-free, with doors closed when no trailer is docked. The manoeuvring area, waiting area, 1.2 m walkways with yellow barriers, crossings and dock ramps are confirmed clear, marked and lit, with the 8 km/h hall, 15 km/h yard and 5 km/h shared-area limits signposted.

5. Zone E cold-zone verification is performed manually each shift. The shift team reads the independent thermometer, confirms the store is held between +2 °C and +8 °C, checks that continuous monitoring and audible alarms are active, confirms doors self-close and seals are intact, and records time, temperature, name and any alarm or excursion in the cold log under PR-12. Any deviation stops moves in Zone E and is escalated to the shift supervisor at once.

6. Storage and handling zones are walked each shift. Zone A unloading lanes and inspection stations, Zone B racking aisles of 3.0 m and main aisles of 4.0 m, Zone C pick faces and flow racks, Zone D staging lanes for doors 5-8 with its 2 stretch wrappers, and Zone F packing stations, quarantine area and 60 m2 ventilated hazmat cage are confirmed clear of obstructions, spills, waste and unassigned pallets. Rack damage, barrier damage, blocked sprinklers and over-height block stacks above 3 pallets or 4.0 m are reported the same shift.

7. Load, quarantine and hazmat status is verified each shift. The supervisor confirms that put-away respects the 800 kg pallet limit and the 2,700 kg rack-bay limit, that hazmat sits only in the cage and at no more than 4,000 kg, that damaged goods found are in quarantine the same day, and that the cardboard baler area is clear and guarded. Counts in progress on the daily rotating cycle-count schedule, second counts outstanding and adjustments held pending recount are confirmed with the stock controllers.

8. People readiness and close-down complete the per-shift cycle. At start-up the supervisor confirms staffing against roster, floater deployment, high-visibility vests and class S3 footwear on everyone on the floor, and seat-belt use on moving forklifts under PR-10 and PR-11. At 14:00 work in progress is carried forward, and at 22:00, and at the end of any approved Saturday morning overtime shift, the supervisor confirms aisles clear, doors 1-8 closed with levellers parked, powered equipment keyed off and on charge, quarantine and hazmat cage locked, and Zone E monitoring continuing before the building is locked.

title: Arrival and scheduling
text:
1. All inbound deliveries arrive only through advance scheduling by the dispatcher under PR-01. The dispatcher books transport with the carrier, allocates a numbered inbound door from doors 1-4 and a fixed time slot, and communicates both before the vehicle departs for Port Sellow. No inbound truck is promised a door or slot by any other role.

2. Time slots are planned against Zone A capacity and shift hours. Inbound slots fall inside the morning shift 06:00-14:00 and the afternoon shift 14:00-22:00, Monday to Friday, plus Saturday morning overtime when approved. The dispatcher sequences arrivals so that unloading lanes, inspection stations and inbound operators in Zone A are available, and staggers carriers to keep the 3,500 m2 yard manoeuvring area and the dock approaches clear.

3. On arrival the driver reports to the controlled gate, states carrier, client, purchase order reference, assigned door and slot time, and presents the transport documents for gate confirmation. The gate directs the vehicle either to the assigned door when free and called, or to the marked waiting area. Entry and exit follow the fixed one-way circulation at 15 km/h, reducing to 5 km/h at crossings and dock ramps.

4. Trucks without a valid slot, arriving early, arriving late, or arriving at the wrong door are not docked on arrival. They wait in the marked driver waiting area until the dispatcher reassigns them to a free inbound door and slot. Shift supervisors, forklift operators and inbound operators do not change door allocations, do not wave trucks to doors, and refer every exception to the dispatcher.

5. Docking takes place only at doors 1-4, which open directly into Zone A receiving. When called, the trailer reverses to the assigned leveller, is chocked and secured, and the driver secures the vehicle. Drivers remain in the cab during docking or, if required to leave the cab, remain in the marked waiting area and the marked dock-side pedestrian bay. Drivers never enter the hall or Zone A.

6. The document-first rule applies to every inbound load without exception. Nothing is unloaded until the delivery documents have been presented at the door and checked by the inbound operator. The trailer doors may be opened for identity check, but no pallet, carton or unit is moved off the trailer, and no unloading equipment is positioned, before the paperwork check is complete and passed.

7. The document check confirms trailer and carrier identity against the dispatcher slot, delivery note against purchase order and client booking, article numbers, quantities, batch and expiry data where required, and visible transport damage or seal irregularity. Only when document, slot and load agree does the inbound operator authorise unloading to start and record start time, door, carrier and reference in the receiving log.

8. If documents are missing, incomplete, do not match the booking, or show goods that were not ordered, unloading does not start. The goods stay on the trailer, the trailer stays on its door or is moved back to the waiting area on dispatcher instruction, and the inbound operator escalates to the shift supervisor and dispatcher the same shift. Nothing moves past Zone A until the paperwork is checked and corrected.

9. Every arrival, slot use and document result is recorded for handover. The dispatcher log holds door, slot, carrier, arrival and departure times and reassignments, and the Zone A receiving log holds document-check outcome and release to unload. Both feed the PR-15 end-of-shift handover, so trucks docked across the 14:00 or 22:00 changeover stay on their assigned door and slot under dispatcher control until unloading and inspection are complete.

title: Unloading and inspection
text:
### ops.ch04.s2 Unloading and inspection

1. Unloading starts only after the document check under PR-01 is passed and recorded. The inbound operator at doors 1-4 confirms door, carrier, slot and paperwork agreement in the receiving log, authorises start, and positions unloading equipment. No pallet, carton or unit is moved off the trailer before that authorisation, and the trailer remains chocked and secured on its leveller throughout.

2. Unloading is carried out by inbound operators with forklift operators in support. The 6 counterbalance forklifts rated at 2.5 t, the 8 electric pallet jacks and the 12 hand pallet jacks are used according to load and lane, driven only by warehouse-manager-authorised operators after the documented check before first use each day. Levellers bridging the 1.2 m dock height are operated only by trained operators, with dock doors open only while the assigned trailer is docked.

3. All unloading work stays inside Zone A receiving of 800 m2. Unloaded goods are placed directly into the marked unloading lanes and inspection stations for that door, clear of the 4.0 m main transport aisles, walkways and dock approaches. Zone A is not used for storage: goods wait there only for counting, inspection and system booking, and nothing leaves Zone A for Zone B, E or F until booking is complete.

4. Every delivery is counted as it is unloaded. The inbound operator counts pallets, cartons and units by delivery note and purchase order, checks article numbers, quantities, batch and expiry data where required, and records the count in the receiving log. Forklift operators do not remove counted pallets from the inspection station until the inbound operator confirms the count for that pallet.

5. Every delivery is inspected for condition immediately after counting. Packaging integrity, labelling, visible damage, leakage, contamination, odour and, where applicable, temperature evidence and cold-chain labelling are checked at the inspection tables before any booking. Only inspected goods are presented for booking into the system; uninspected goods are not booked and not put away.

6. Safety and segregation apply throughout unloading and inspection. Everyone on the floor wears high-visibility vests and class S3 safety footwear, forklift operators wear seat belts when moving, and powered equipment observes 8 km/h inside the hall and 5 km/h at crossings and dock ramps. Pedestrians use only the 1.2 m walkways with yellow barriers. Spills, debris and broken packaging are cleared before work continues and reported to the shift supervisor.

7. Shortages, overages, wrong articles, batch or expiry mismatches and visible transport damage are stopped at the station. The goods stay in Zone A, are marked and held separately from passed goods, and the inbound operator escalates to the shift supervisor and dispatcher the same shift. The trailer is not released as complete and the load is not booked until the discrepancy is resolved or formally recorded as short, over or damaged.

8. Damaged or suspect goods go to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found under PR-09. They are labelled with date, door, carrier, reference and fault, moved by pallet jack or forklift respecting the 800 kg pallet limit, and entered in the quarantine record. Returns, cold-chain goods needing +2 °C to +8 °C and hazmat for the 60 m2 ventilated cage are segregated at inspection and moved only by the approved route without mixing with general stock.

9. Completion of unloading and inspection is recorded for booking and handover. The receiving log holds door, carrier, reference, start and finish times, counted quantities, inspection result and quarantine moves, and feeds the PR-15 handover. Trailers remain on their assigned door and slot under dispatcher control until the inbound operator confirms unloading and inspection complete, and trucks docked across the 14:00 or 22:00 changeover are handed over with their log status intact.

title: Booking and release
text:
1. Only inspected goods are booked into the system, and only booked goods are released to put-away. No pallet, carton or unit leaves Zone A for Zone B, E or F until counting and inspection under PR-01 are complete and the system receipt is posted. Uninspected, uncounted or document-failed goods are never booked and never moved past Zone A.

2. Booking is performed at the Zone A booking points by the inbound operator immediately after inspection is passed. The receipt is posted in the WMS on the shared handheld scanners, against the purchase order and client booking for that door, carrier and slot. The operator confirms article numbers, counted quantities, batch and expiry data where required, and condition status before posting.

3. Each booked pallet receives its system identity at booking. The WMS generates a pallet licence plate with article, quantity, batch, expiry, receipt date, door and reference, which is printed, fixed to the pallet, and scan-verified before the pallet leaves the inspection station. Pallets without a verified label stay in Zone A and are not presented for put-away.

4. Booking assigns the put-away destination under PR-02. General reserve stock is directed to Zone B bulk storage, temperature-sensitive goods to Zone E cold zone between +2 °C and +8 °C, permitted hazmat to the 60 m2 ventilated cage in Zone F, and value-added or controlled stock to Zone F services. The WMS proposes a location respecting the 800 kg pallet limit, the 2,700 kg rack-bay limit and the 4,000 kg cage limit, and the inbound operator accepts or escalates it.

5. Release to put-away is a separate confirmation after booking. The inbound operator checks that all pallets for the line are labelled, scan-readable and staged clear of the 4.0 m main aisles and walkways, records booked quantities and destinations in the receiving log, and releases the pallets to forklift operators for put-away. Forklift operators collect only released, labelled pallets and scan them out of Zone A on pickup.

6. Segregated goods follow their own booking route without mixing. Cold-chain pallets are booked with temperature evidence and moved first to Zone E by the closed route with doors kept shut. Hazmat pallets are booked only up to cage capacity and moved directly to the cage. Damaged or suspect pallets are not booked as available stock and go to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found, entered in the quarantine record under PR-09.

7. Shortages, overages, wrong articles and batch or expiry mismatches stop booking for that line. The goods stay in Zone A marked and held apart, the system receipt is posted only for the passed quantity where the WMS permits a short receipt, and the discrepancy is escalated the same shift to the shift supervisor and dispatcher. The trailer is not released as complete until the discrepancy is resolved or formally recorded.

8. Completion closes the inbound control for that load. The receiving log holds document result, counted and booked quantities, labels issued, put-away destinations released, quarantine moves, and start and finish times per door. Stock controllers verify booked receipts against system stock during the daily cycle-count schedule, and open receipts, unreleased pallets and delayed trailers are carried into the PR-15 handover with door and slot intact under dispatcher control.

title: Bulk storage put-away
text:
### ops.ch05.s1 Bulk storage put-away

1. Only booked goods are put away to Zone B under PR-02. Forklift operators collect pallets in Zone A only after the inbound operator has posted the system receipt, fixed the WMS pallet licence plate, and released the pallet for put-away. Pallets without a scan-verified label, uninspected goods, and goods with unresolved document discrepancies stay in Zone A and are never moved to bulk storage.

2. The WMS assigns every pallet a put-away location before transport. General reserve stock is directed to Zone B bulk storage of 2,200 m2, with temperature-sensitive goods to Zone E and permitted hazmat to the ventilated cage in Zone F excluded from this flow. The operator accepts the proposed rack position or stack mark, respecting the 800 kg limit per pallet including load, and scans the pallet out of Zone A on pickup and into its location on placement.

3. High-bay pallet racking in Zone B provides 2,400 pallet positions and is served only by the 4 reach trucks rated at 1.6 t. The 6 counterbalance forklifts rated at 2.5 t handle horizontal transport to the aisle ends and block-stack placement. No person drives either type without warehouse-manager authorisation under PR-10 and without the documented check before first use each day.

4. Each rack bay carries at most 2,700 kg in total. With the site-wide limit of 800 kg per pallet including load, no bay holds more than three full-weight pallets, and the WMS blocks any fourth placement that would exceed the bay limit. Operators verify bay load plates, never force oversize or overweight pallets into racking, and escalate any system proposal that appears to overload a bay to the shift supervisor and stock controllers.

5. Free block-stacking outside racking is permitted only in marked stack positions in Zone B. Stacks are limited to 3 pallets high and 4.0 m total height including pallets, whichever is reached first. Block stacks stand clear of the 4.0 m main transport aisles, the 3.0 m rack storage aisles, pedestrian walkways, dock approaches, sprinkler clearance, and marked fire and evacuation routes.

6. Movements inside Zone B observe the fixed aisle and speed system. Powered trucks travel at 8 km/h inside the hall and at 5 km/h at crossings, pedestrian zones and dock ramps, using only the 4.0 m main aisles for travel and entering 3.0 m rack aisles only for placement and retrieval. Pedestrians use only the 1.2 m walkways separated by yellow barriers. Everyone on the floor wears high-visibility vests and class S3 safety footwear, and forklift operators wear seat belts when moving.

7. Every put-away is scan-confirmed at the location. The operator scans the pallet licence plate and the location label, confirms article, quantity, batch and expiry match the booking, and reports any location occupied, damaged, mislabelled or system-mismatched stock to the shift supervisor and stock controllers before placing elsewhere. Pallets are placed squarely, fully supported on beams or stack base, with labels facing the aisle.

8. Completion closes the put-away task in the WMS and the receiving log. Damaged pallets, collapsed loads or leaking units found during put-away are not racked and go to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found under PR-09, entered in the quarantine record. Open put-away tasks, blocked locations and rack damage are reported the same shift to the shift supervisor and maintenance technician and carried into the PR-15 handover.

title: Cold-zone storage
text:
### ops.ch05.s2 Cold-zone storage

1. Zone E is the enclosed chilled store of 300 m2 for temperature-sensitive packed goods only. It is held continuously between +2 °C and +8 °C with continuous electronic monitoring and audible alarms, backed by a manual temperature verification by the shift team each shift under PR-12. No ambient goods, hazmat, quarantine stock or packing materials are stored in Zone E.

2. Only booked cold-chain goods enter Zone E under PR-02. Forklift operators collect pallets in Zone A only after the inbound operator has posted the system receipt with temperature evidence, fixed the WMS pallet licence plate, and released the pallet for Zone E. Pallets without a scan-verified label, with missing batch or expiry data, or with unresolved document discrepancies stay in Zone A and are never moved to the cold zone.

3. Cold-chain pallets move first and by the closed route. On release they are taken directly from Zone A to Zone E without staging in Zone B, C, D or F, clear of the 4.0 m main transport aisles and pedestrian walkways. Doors of Zone E are kept closed except for the put-away, replenishment or check in progress, and are confirmed self-closing and sealed after each move.

4. The WMS assigns every cold-chain pallet its storage location before transport. The operator respects the site-wide limit of 800 kg per pallet including load, scans the pallet out of Zone A on pickup and scans pallet and location on placement, and places pallets squarely, fully supported, with labels facing the aisle. Any location occupied, damaged, mislabelled or system-mismatched is reported to the shift supervisor and stock controllers before placing elsewhere.

5. Storage conditions are maintained without interruption. The store remains between +2 °C and +8 °C at all times, including nights, shift changeovers at 06:00, 14:00 and 22:00, and any approved Saturday morning overtime. Power, refrigeration, monitoring and alarms stay active when the hall is otherwise closed and locked, and Zone E stock is never left on dock ramps, in Zone A lanes or in uncooled staging.

6. Each shift verifies Zone E under PR-12 and PR-15. The shift team reads the independent thermometer, confirms monitoring and alarms active, checks door closure, seals and lights, and records time, temperature, name and any alarm in the cold log. Any deviation, excursion, door fault, ice build-up, water, odour or packaging failure stops all moves in Zone E at once and is escalated the same shift to the shift supervisor, stock controllers and maintenance technician.

7. Damaged, leaking, thaw-suspect or temperature-abused goods leave the cold chain the same day they are found under PR-09. They are labelled with date, location, reference and fault, moved to quarantine in Zone F for decision, and entered in the quarantine record. They are never re-cooled, re-racked in Zone E or picked for orders. Replenishment to Zone C pick faces is fed only from released, in-temperature stock on WMS task.

8. Accuracy, hygiene and repair in Zone E are controlled daily. Stock controllers include Zone E in the daily rotating cycle-count schedule with no adjustment without a second count, and open tasks, blocked locations and excursions are carried into the PR-15 handover. Everyone entering wears high-visibility vests and class S3 safety footwear, powered trucks observe 8 km/h inside and 5 km/h at crossings, and any rack, door, sensor or alarm fault is reported the same shift to the shift supervisor and maintenance technician and logged as a repair.

title: Hazmat cage and quarantine
text:
### ops.ch05.s3 Hazmat cage and quarantine

1. Zone F services and control of 600 m2 holds two controlled stores under PR-09 and PR-13: the separate ventilated hazmat cage of 60 m2 and the quarantine area for damaged and suspect goods. Both are marked, signed, kept locked, and recorded on the site plan. No other part of the hall is used for either purpose.

2. The hazmat cage is the only place hazmat may sit. Permitted packed hazmat for regular clients is stored only inside the cage, never in Zone A, B, C, D or E, never on aisles, dock ramps or staging lanes, and never in general quarantine. Any hazmat pallet found outside the cage is moved there at once or, if the cage is full or the goods are damaged, secured, reported to the shift supervisor, and handled as a spill or quarantine case the same shift.

3. The cage holds at most 4,000 kg at a time. With the site-wide limit of 800 kg per pallet including load, this means at most 5 full-weight pallets in the cage. The WMS blocks any booking that would exceed the cage limit, and inbound operators do not book hazmat without available cage capacity. Open cage quantity is confirmed each shift and carried into the PR-15 handover.

4. Only booked hazmat enters the cage under PR-02 and PR-13. Forklift operators collect pallets in Zone A only after the inbound operator has posted the system receipt, fixed the WMS pallet licence plate, and released the pallet for the cage. Pallets without a scan-verified label, with missing hazard labels or safety data, or with unresolved document discrepancies stay in Zone A and are never moved to Zone F.

5. Hazmat moves go direct and segregated. On release pallets are taken directly from Zone A to the cage without staging, clear of the 4.0 m main aisles and pedestrian walkways, with powered trucks at 8 km/h inside and 5 km/h at crossings and ramps. The operator scans pallet and cage location on placement, places pallets squarely and fully supported with hazard labels facing the aisle, and confirms ventilation running, doors self-closing, and incompatible goods separated.

6. The quarantine area in Zone F holds all damaged, leaking, suspect and temperature-abused goods after they are found the same day. Goods found in Zone A, B, C, D or E are labelled with date, location, reference and fault, moved the same day respecting the 800 kg pallet limit, and entered in the quarantine record under PR-09. Quarantined pallets are never racked, picked, re-cooled or dispatched before a decision.

7. Quarantine stock stays under stock-controller control. Returns and packing staff propose restock, rework or scrap only after inspection of every unit under PR-07, stock controllers hold the system block so quarantined quantities are not available to promise, and no unit leaves quarantine until the shift supervisor approves the final disposition. Cases needing write-off above 500 EUR are secured, documented and passed to the warehouse manager the same day; split write-offs are not permitted.

8. Safety, spill response and handover close the controls. Everyone in Zone F wears high-visibility vests and class S3 safety footwear, plus task PPE for spill handling, and forklift operators wear seat belts when moving. Spills, leaks, odours and damaged packaging stop work, trigger the PR-13 spill response under the shift supervisor, and are reported and logged for the maintenance technician the same shift. Cage quantity, quarantine bookings, faults and open decisions are recorded in the shift file and carried into the PR-15 handover.

title: Replenishment of pick faces
text:
### ops.ch06.s1 Replenishment of pick faces

1. Zone C pick faces are replenished from bulk before each picking shift under PR-03. Ground-level pick faces and flow racks in Zone C of 1,200 m2 are fed only from Zone B bulk storage, and cold pick faces only from Zone E, so that pickers start every shift with released, system-available stock in position. No picking task starts on an empty or unreplenished face.

2. Replenishment runs only on WMS task. Stock controllers release replenishment needs from open customer orders, minimum levels and booked receipts, and the WMS proposes source pallets in Zone B or Zone E with article, quantity, batch and expiry. Forklift operators collect only the tasked source pallet and quantity, and do not top up faces on their own judgement.

3. Source pallets are retrieved and confirmed by scan. The operator drives the 4 reach trucks rated at 1.6 t in the high bays and the 6 counterbalance forklifts rated at 2.5 t for horizontal transport, only with warehouse-manager authorisation and after the documented check before first use each day. Pallet licence plate and source location are scanned on pickup, respecting the 800 kg pallet limit and the 2,700 kg rack-bay limit, and any location mismatch, damage or system error is reported to the shift supervisor and stock controllers before moving.

4. Transport to Zone C goes direct to the assigned face. Pallets move via the 4.0 m main transport aisles at 8 km/h inside the hall and 5 km/h at crossings, pedestrian zones and dock ramps, clear of the 1.2 m walkways with yellow barriers. Replenishment stock is never staged in Zone D, never left in aisles, and cold-chain pallets move first by the closed route with Zone E doors kept shut.

5. Placement follows the face limit and rotation. The operator scans face location and pallet, confirms article, batch and expiry match the task, places full pallets, cartons or units within the marked face quantity without overfilling, crushing or blocking labels, and keeps older batch and earlier expiry to the front. Overstock stays in its bulk location in Zone B or Zone E and is not forced onto the face.

6. Cold and special goods keep their segregation during replenishment. Cold faces are fed only from released, in-temperature stock between +2 °C and +8 °C on WMS task, hazmat is never used for general pick-face feed and stays only in the 60 m2 cage up to 4,000 kg, and any damaged, leaking or temperature-abused unit found during replenishment goes to quarantine in Zone F the same day under PR-09 and is entered in the quarantine record.

7. Safety and order apply throughout the feed. Everyone on the floor wears high-visibility vests and class S3 safety footwear, forklift operators wear seat belts when moving, and flow-rack, beam and face damage, spills and broken packaging stop the task until the shift supervisor and maintenance technician are informed the same shift. Empty pallets, wrap and waste are removed to their marks so pick faces and aisle ends stay clear.

8. Completion is scan-closed and handed over. The operator confirms face quantity in the WMS on the shared handheld scanners, the receiving log and cycle-count schedule are left consistent by the stock controllers with no adjustment without a second count, and open replenishment tasks, blocked faces, short bulk positions and rack damage are recorded in the shift file and carried into the PR-15 handover for the next picking shift.

title: Order picking
text:
### ops.ch06.s2 Order picking

1. Order picking takes place only in Zone C of 1,200 m2 under PR-04. Ground-level pick faces and flow racks, fed from Zone B bulk storage and for cold faces from Zone E, are the only pick locations. No picking takes place from reserve racking, from Zone A, Zone D staging, quarantine or the 60 m2 hazmat cage. Pickers start work only on faces replenished before the picking shift.

2. Picking runs only on WMS scanner tasks. The ten pickers work across morning 06:00-14:00 and afternoon 14:00-22:00 shifts against tasks released by the stock controllers from open customer orders. Each task states article, quantity, batch and expiry, pick-face location and destination in Zone D. Pickers collect only the tasked quantity from the tasked face and do not pick on memory, paper or judgement.

3. Pickers use the 20 shared handheld WMS scanners signed out at shift start. They log in, accept one task at a time, scan the face location label, then scan each article or carton picked. The scanner confirms article, batch and expiry match and blocks wrong picks, short faces and blocked stock. Any scanner, label or system mismatch stops that pick until the shift supervisor and stock controllers resolve it.

4. Every picked item is scan-verified before it is packed. The picker scans item against task, checks condition, count and date, keeps older batch and earlier expiry to the front under rotation, and places goods squarely on the order pallet or tote without crushing, overhang or mixed batches. Unverified, damaged or leaking units are never packed for the order and go to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found under PR-09.

5. Picked orders are packed, labelled and moved to Zone D as completed units. The picker confirms task-complete in the WMS, fixes the order label with client, order, destination and pallet identity, leaves the face clean and faced up, and moves labelled pallets with hand pallet jacks or calls a forklift operator for powered moves. Only labelled, system-confirmed units leave Zone C for Zone D.

6. Shortages, empty faces, wrong stock and damage stop the task at the face. The picker leaves the face marked, records short, damaged or mislocated quantity in the scanner, and reports at once to the shift supervisor in charge and the stock controllers. The face is not topped up by the picker and no substitution is made. Replenishment is re-tasked from Zone B or Zone E, and adjustments are never posted without a second count under PR-08.

7. Cold and special goods keep segregation during picking. Cold orders are picked only from released, in-temperature faces between +2 °C and +8 °C with Zone E doors kept shut, and move first by the closed route to Zone D without staging in ambient aisles. Hazmat is never picked to general faces. Damaged, thaw-suspect or temperature-abused units are labelled with date, face, reference and fault and entered in the quarantine record.

8. Safety, order and handover close every picking period. Everyone on the floor wears high-visibility vests and class S3 safety footwear, powered equipment observes 8 km/h inside the hall and 5 km/h at crossings, pedestrian zones and ramps, and pedestrians use only the 1.2 m walkways with yellow barriers clear of the 4.0 m main aisles. Open scanner tasks, short faces, quarantine moves and face or rack damage are recorded in the shift file and carried into the PR-15 handover.

title: Packing and labelling
text:
### ops.ch07.s1 Packing and labelling

1. Packing and labelling takes place after scan-verified picking under PR-05. Only picked units that have been scan-verified in Zone C against the WMS scanner task move to packing. Unverified, short-picked, wrong-batch or damaged units are never packed for dispatch and go to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found under PR-09.

2. Packing is performed at the packing positions at the Zone C aisle ends and in Zone D dispatch of 900 m2. Pickers confirm task-complete in the WMS on the 20 shared handheld scanners, build stable order pallets and cartons without crushing, overhang or mixed batches, and keep older batch and earlier expiry separated. Pallets are built within the site-wide limit of 800 kg per pallet including load.

3. Every packed unit passes a final scan check before labelling. The packer scans the face-pick quantity, article, batch and expiry against the customer order, checks count and condition, and confirms the WMS order line as packed. Any mismatch, shortage, mislabelled carton or system block stops that unit at the packing position until the shift supervisor and stock controllers resolve it.

4. Each packed pallet and carton receives its outbound label at packing. The WMS generates the order label with client, order number, destination, article and quantity, batch and expiry where required, and pallet licence identity, which is printed, fixed squarely and scan-verified for readability before the unit leaves the packing position. Units without a verified label stay out of Zone D staging and are never wrapped as finished loads.

5. Wrapped, labelled pallets only are staged for dispatch. Packed, labelled pallets move to Zone D and are wrapped on the 2 semi-automatic stretch wrappers to a stable, fully enclosed load with base, corners and top secured and labels left readable. The wrapper stations stand in the marked lanes for doors 5-8 clear of the 4.0 m main aisles, walkways and dock approaches, and are operated only by trained staff.

6. Segregation is maintained through packing, labelling and wrapping. Cold-chain orders move first by the closed route and are packed and wrapped without breaking the +2 °C to +8 °C chain and without ambient staging. Hazmat is never packed to general pallets and stays only in the 60 m2 ventilated cage up to 4,000 kg. Damaged, leaking or temperature-abused units found at packing are labelled with date, order, reference and fault and entered in the quarantine record.

7. Safety and order apply at all packing and wrapping positions. Everyone on the floor wears high-visibility vests and class S3 safety footwear, forklift operators wear seat belts when moving, and powered equipment observes 8 km/h inside the hall and 5 km/h at crossings, pedestrian zones and dock ramps. Pedestrians use only the 1.2 m walkways with yellow barriers. Film cores, strapping, waste cardboard and empty pallets are removed to their marks, with waste to the cardboard baler area.

8. Completion is scan-closed and handed over. The packer confirms packed, labelled and wrapped quantities in the WMS, places only finished pallets in the marked staging lane for the assigned outbound door 5-8, and records open order lines, short quantities, re-wraps, printer and wrapper faults and quarantine moves in the shift file. Unreleased pallets, rewraps and faults are carried into the PR-15 handover and no pallet is loaded until the dispatcher releases the load under PR-06.

title: Staging and loading
text:
### ops.ch07.s2 Staging and loading

1. Zone D dispatch of 900 m2 in front of outbound doors 5-8 is the only staging and loading area under PR-06. It holds marked staging lanes per door, final-check positions and the 2 semi-automatic stretch wrappers. Only wrapped, labelled and system-released pallets are staged here, allocated to their assigned door and time slot. No inbound goods or unwrapped stock are held in Zone D.

2. Staging runs only on dispatcher instruction. The dispatcher books transport, assigns every carrier outbound door 5-8 and time slot, and releases each load from Zone D by WMS. Pickers and forklift operators place finished pallets only in the marked lane for the door stated on the task, clear of the 4.0 m main aisles, 1.2 m walkways with yellow barriers and dock approaches.

3. Every staged pallet is verified at the lane. The team scans pallet licence and outbound label on the shared handheld scanners, confirms client, order, destination, quantity and pallet identity against the released load, checks wrap intact with labels readable, and respects the 800 kg limit per pallet including load. Pallets without a verified label or not on the released load stay apart and are never loaded.

4. Trucks are called from the marked waiting area only when the lane is complete and the load is released. The trailer reverses to the assigned leveller bridging the 1.2 m dock height, is chocked and secured, and remains on that door and slot under dispatcher control. Drivers remain in the cab or in the marked waiting area and dock-side pedestrian bay and never enter the hall or Zone D.

5. Loading starts only after release. Forklift operators, authorised by the warehouse manager with the documented check before first use each day, load with the 6 counterbalance forklifts rated at 2.5 t and electric pallet jacks, driven at 8 km/h inside and 5 km/h at crossings, pedestrian zones and dock ramps. Levellers and doors are operated only by trained operators, with doors open only while the assigned trailer is docked.

6. Loading follows the load plan in release order. Operators scan each pallet out of Zone D on loading, build stable floor positions without overhang, crushing or mixing orders, and confirm trailer identity throughout. No pallet is added, removed or restaged after release without a new dispatcher instruction, and trucks docked across the 14:00 or 22:00 changeover stay on their door under dispatcher control.

7. Completion is checked before sealing. The dispatcher or shift supervisor confirms staged quantity against loaded quantity in the WMS, count of pallets, order completeness, and condition of wrap and labels, resolving any short, over or damaged pallet in quarantine in Zone F the same day under PR-09. The load is not closed with open lines or unverified pallets on board.

8. Every outbound trailer is sealed and recorded before departure. The dispatcher confirms trailer identity, fits and records the seal number, posts despatch in the WMS with door, carrier, time and seal, authorises departure, and carries open loads, delayed carriers and seal records into the PR-15 handover. Everyone on the floor wears high-visibility vests and class S3 safety footwear, with seat belts worn on moving forklifts.

title: Load and capacity limits
text:
1. Every load planned from Zone D respects the site-wide pallet limit first. A pallet, load included, may weigh at most 800 kg. That figure is the basis for all trailer, van, rack and cage capacities on site. No order pallet is built, wrapped, staged or loaded above 800 kg, and any unit exceeding it is split, repacked or replanned before release.

2. The contracted curtain-side trailer is the standard outbound unit. Each trailer carries at most 22,000 kg on 33 floor positions. Weight governs before floor space: at full 800 kg per pallet, weight is reached at 27 pallets while 6 floor positions remain unused. The dispatcher plans every trailer load against both limits together and never promises a 28th full-weight pallet on one trailer.

3. Trailer loads are therefore planned as 27 full-weight pallets maximum. Lighter pallets may use more of the 33 floor positions, but only while total weight stays at or below 22,000 kg and every pallet stays at or below 800 kg. Floor positions are loaded stably without overhang, crushing or mixing unreleased orders, and the load plan states pallet count, total weight and position use for release under PR-06.

4. The delivery van is limited to small drops only. It carries at most 1,200 kg on 6 floor positions. At full 800 kg per pallet this means one full-weight pallet, with the remaining capacity usable only for light cartons or units up to the 1,200 kg total. Anything heavier than the van limit, and any requirement for more than one full-weight pallet, goes by trailer and is not split across van trips to avoid the limit.

5. Van loads are released separately from trailer loads. The dispatcher confirms van identity, planned weight and position count before release, and the team scans each unit out of Zone D on loading. No additional pallet, carton or unit is added after release without a new dispatcher instruction, and over-weight or over-position vans are not sealed or authorised to depart.

6. Per-door throughput caps what dispatch can promise per shift. Each of the 4 outbound doors 5-8 handles at most 3 trailer loads per shift within the morning 06:00-14:00 and afternoon 14:00-22:00 windows. Turnaround includes docking at the 1.2 m leveller, check of wrap and labels, scan-loading, sealing and departure, with doors closed when no trailer is docked.

7. Per-shift site capacity follows directly from the door rate and the trailer weight limit. Four doors at 3 loads each give 12 trailer loads per shift, and 12 loads at 27 full-weight pallets give 324 full-weight pallets per shift. That is the most the site can promise a client for one shift. The dispatcher does not book slots beyond 12 trailer departures per shift, and the shift supervisor sequences Zone C completion, wrapping on the 2 stretch wrappers and Zone D staging to that ceiling.

8. Special limits sit inside the trailer and shift ceilings and never extend them. The 60 m2 ventilated hazmat cage in Zone F holds at most 4,000 kg at a time, which means at most 5 full-weight pallets awaiting or feeding dispatch. Cold-chain orders between +2 °C and +8 °C move first by the closed route but count identically toward trailer weight, positions and the 324-pallet shift total. Open loads, delayed carriers and weight or position exceptions are recorded in the shift file and carried into the PR-15 handover.

title: MHE fleet
text:
### ops.ch08.s1 MHE fleet

1. The site operates an all-electric materials-handling fleet for all internal transport between Zones A to F and the docks. The fleet consists of 6 counterbalance forklifts rated at 2.5 t for general work, 4 reach trucks rated at 1.6 t for the high bays, 8 electric pallet jacks for horizontal moves, and 12 hand pallet jacks for small moves. No diesel, gas or other powered trucks are used on site.

2. Each truck type has a fixed role. The 6 counterbalance forklifts handle unloading support in Zone A, horizontal transport to Zone B aisle ends, block-stack placement, replenishment transport to Zone C, and loading at outbound doors 5-8. The 4 reach trucks work only in the high-bay racking in Zone B with its 2,400 pallet positions. Electric pallet jacks cover dock lanes, inspection stations and short transfers, and hand pallet jacks cover order build and packing positions.

3. All ratings are observed with the site-wide pallet limit. A pallet, load included, may weigh at most 800 kg, so every powered truck is rated above the heaviest single pallet it may carry. Counterbalance capacity at 2.5 t and reach capacity at 1.6 t do not authorise double-pallet handling or overloading, and operators respect bay, attachment and height limits in addition to truck rating.

4. No person drives independently until authorised. Only the warehouse manager authorises new forklift operators, separately for counterbalance forklift, reach truck and electric pallet jack, under PR-10. Authorisation is recorded before first use. Floaters and other staff do not drive powered trucks unless separately authorised for that type, and pickers and packers use hand pallet jacks only for their assigned moves.

5. Every powered truck and every hand pallet jack receives a documented check before its first use each day. The assigned operator inspects brakes, steering, lights, horn, seat belt, forks, chains, mast, wheels, battery charge and leaks on counterbalance and reach trucks, controls, tiller, brakes, wheels and battery on electric pallet jacks, and wheels, forks and hydraulics on hand pallet jacks. The result is recorded with date, truck identity, operator name and signature.

6. Faults stop the truck. Any defect found at check or during the shift is reported at once to the shift supervisor in charge and the maintenance technician, and the truck is tagged out and parked clear of the 4.0 m main aisles, the 3.0 m rack aisles and dock approaches until repaired and logged. Unsafe trucks are never handed over as available, and the tag is removed only by the maintenance technician after repair.

7. Batteries, charging and parking are controlled each shift. Trucks are charged only in the marked charging positions clear of walkways and staging, with cables routed off pedestrian routes. At 14:00 trucks pass to the next shift with charge status in the PR-15 handover, and at 22:00, and at the end of any approved Saturday morning overtime shift, powered equipment is keyed off, secured and left on charge. Keys are removed and trucks are never left unattended with power on.

8. Use on the floor follows the aisle, speed and PPE system. Powered trucks travel on 4.0 m main aisles at 8 km/h inside the hall and at 5 km/h at crossings, marked pedestrian zones and dock ramps, entering 3.0 m rack aisles only for placement and retrieval. Everyone on the floor wears high-visibility vests and class S3 safety footwear, forklift operators wear seat belts whenever the truck is moving, and pedestrians use only the 1.2 m walkways separated by yellow barriers.

9. Availability, faults and checks are recorded for handover and maintenance. The shift file holds daily check sheets, tag-outs, battery and damage reports, and the maintenance log holds every repair with date, equipment, fault and action, including the monthly documented racking safety inspection where truck impact is found. Open faults, swapped trucks and outstanding checks are carried into the PR-15 handover so the next shift starts only on checked, authorised equipment.

title: Aisles and speed limits
text:
### ops.ch08.s2 Aisles and speed limits

1. Internal transport uses a fixed aisle system that separates powered equipment from pedestrians throughout the hall and yard. Main transport aisles of 4.0 m width carry forklifts, reach trucks and pallet jacks between Zones A to F and docks 1-8. Rack storage aisles in Zone B bulk storage of 3.0 m width serve placement and retrieval only. No other routes are used for powered travel.

2. Main aisles of 4.0 m are kept clear at all times. They provide two-way travel for the 6 counterbalance forklifts rated at 2.5 t, the 8 electric pallet jacks and loaded hand pallet jacks, with passing clearance for the widest 800 kg pallet. No staging, block-stacking, charging, waste, empty pallets or parked trucks are placed in main aisles, at aisle junctions, or across dock approaches.

3. Rack aisles of 3.0 m in Zone B are working aisles, not travel routes. Only the 4 reach trucks rated at 1.6 t enter for high-bay placement and retrieval at the 2,400 pallet positions, and counterbalance trucks enter only to the aisle end for handover and block-stack work in marked positions. Trucks enter an occupied rack aisle only after eye contact and horn signal, and pedestrians do not enter rack aisles while a reach truck is operating inside.

4. Pedestrians move only on designated walkways of 1.2 m width. Walkways run along main aisles, between zones, and to the office annex, waiting area and assembly point by the north fence, and are physically separated from truck traffic by yellow barriers. Marked crossings connect walkways across main aisles and at docks 1-8. Pedestrians cross only on crossings and never shortcut through transport or rack aisles.

5. Speed limits are fixed and enforced for all powered equipment and vehicles under PR-10 and PR-11. The limit is 8 km/h inside the building and 15 km/h in the 3,500 m2 fenced yard. Wherever people and trucks meet — in marked pedestrian zones, at crossings, and on the dock ramps at the 1.2 m dock height — the limit is 5 km/h. Limits are signposted at the gate, at hall entrances and at each shared area.

6. The 5 km/h rule governs all shared working. Trucks slow to 5 km/h on approach to every crossing, walkway opening, Zone A inspection area, Zone C pick-face ends, Zone D staging lanes for doors 5-8, Zone F packing and quarantine areas, and dock levellers. Drivers sound the horn before blind corners, rack-aisle entry and dock entry, give way to pedestrians on crossings, and stop where sight lines are blocked until the shift supervisor clears passage.

7. Yard circulation follows the one-way system at 15 km/h, reducing to 5 km/h at crossings and dock ramps. Arriving and departing trailers use the marked manoeuvring lanes clear of the waiting area and walkways. Forklifts do not enter the yard road except to cross at marked points, and pallet jacks do not leave the hall. Trailers dock only at their dispatcher-assigned door from doors 1-4 inbound and doors 5-8 outbound, chocked and on the leveller.

8. Aisles, walkways, crossings and speed signs are checked each shift. The shift supervisor confirms barrier integrity, floor markings readable, crossings unobstructed, mirrors and lighting serviceable, and manoeuvring and waiting areas clear of pallets, wrap, snow, ice, spills and debris. Any damage to barriers, markings, signs, racking uprights or dock equipment is reported the same shift to the shift supervisor and maintenance technician, and the area is coned off until repaired.

9. Breaches stop work. Speeding, leaving marked routes, parking or staging in aisles, walking outside walkways, or removing or driving through barriers are reported to the shift supervisor in charge at once, entered in the incident report, and reviewed before the next shift under PR-15. Repeated breach removes driving authorisation pending warehouse-manager review, and open aisle faults and speed incidents are carried into the PR-15 handover.

title: Dock and packing equipment
text:
### ops.ch08.s3 Dock and packing equipment

1. Dock and packing equipment consists of fixed installations that condition every inbound and outbound move. Each of the 8 dock doors at 1.2 m dock height has its own dock leveller with door seal, traffic light and chock point, Zone D dispatch of 900 m2 holds 2 semi-automatic stretch wrappers, and the site operates 1 cardboard baler for packing waste. No other powered dock or packing plant is used.

2. Dock levellers bridge the 1.2 m height between hall floor and trailer bed at doors 1-4 inbound and doors 5-8 outbound. Levellers are operated only by trained operators authorised for that door, only when the dispatcher-assigned trailer is chocked, braked and confirmed on the leveller. Doors remain closed when no trailer is docked, and levellers are parked flush after each departure.

3. Levellers are checked every shift under PR-06 and PR-10. The shift team confirms deck, lip, hydraulics, controls, traffic lights, seals, chocks and pit clear of debris, with no damage, oil leak or uncontrolled drop. Any fault is reported at once to the shift supervisor in charge and the maintenance technician, the door is taken out of service, coned off, and carried into the PR-15 handover until repaired and logged.

4. The 2 semi-automatic stretch wrappers stand in the marked lanes for doors 5-8 in Zone D. Only wrapped, labelled pallets are staged for dispatch, and wrapping is performed only on these machines to a stable, fully enclosed load with base, corners and top secured and labels left readable. Wrapper stations stand clear of the 4.0 m main aisles, 1.2 m walkways with yellow barriers and dock approaches.
